assessment.area: Current claim and atomic lease eligibility
assessment.evidence: The method requires a live transaction, acquires the shared per-job/key lock through lockIntent, and refuses non-running/missing intent. One MATERIALIZED renewal_clock supplies the UPDATE clock sample. Exact intent/claim ID/BIGINT generation and still-live stored old lease, execution and lifetime are predicates of the write; stale handles do not overwrite a replacement claim. A zero-row result is null, not revival permission.

assessment.area: No budget, fence or dispatch reset
assessment.evidence: SET changes only lease_until. The new lease is min(databaseNow + persisted lease_ms, immutable execution_deadline, immutable lifetime_deadline). The claim ID, generation, invocation count, first claim and all absolute deadlines remain unchanged. Renewal at the invocation cap is permitted only for the same still-live invocation, not a new invocation. possible_dispatch=1 remains 1; renewal cannot reauthorize another checkpoint/send.

assessment.area: Late SQL response and transactional behavior
assessment.evidence: The returned ledger's deadlines are checked against a post-statement database-time sample. Delayed SQL returns no handle after expiry; a surviving renewal is not refunded or converted into new invocation authority. Caller rollback undoes its lease update. Any null/late result leaves the existing claim lifecycle to later checked recovery; it does not assert a provider outcome or release an unknown key.

There is deliberately no max(oldLease, newLease) clamp. A backward database clock sample can shorten the stored lease, but never exceeds the unchanged execution/lifetime caps. The modeled 400ms regression shortened lease by 400ms without changing other fields; a checkpoint with the older cached handle subsequently used the shorter stored lease and rejected. This is not proof of monotonic DB time, no revival after arbitrary physical-clock rollback, host-clock agreement, process preemption or cached worker authority. A current-generation claim remains interpreted by the supported database clock, and a replacement generation still fences out the old handle.

retainedLimits: Storage foundation only: no authored/public/operator or worker-heartbeat binding, provider dispatch, receipt/acknowledgement, scheduler, dead-letter, attempt-history, trusted resolution or full 18-case ASYNC conformance approval. Whole RM-306 remains incomplete. Cancellation additions require their own review.

Assumes the compatible compiler-owned nullable first-claim/lifetime schema and supported DB calendar/arithmetic range. Lazy IF NOT EXISTS supplies no schema attestation, migration from earlier NOT NULL v1 layouts, collision handling or corrupt/restored-record validation. Missing backend, key/foreign-key assumptions and default/golden numeric limits remain separate gates.

Checks establish sampled DB-time eligibility, not a guarantee that a handle stays live through final clock-query latency, caller work, COMMIT or dispatch. A positive result inside the transaction is provisional until commit acknowledgement. Future workers must handle commit uncertainty, revalidate stored current fence/lease/time and never use a cached longer lease as unchecked send authority.

Clock rollback can shorten a lease or alter whether a current-generation timestamp is considered live; no physical-clock-regression or monotonic-wall-clock guarantee is supplied. Immutable caps and fence predicates remain enforced under supported database-time semantics. Database fencing is not exactly-once effect delivery or hard active-call interruption.

The preserved outbox token guards new SQL callback invocation after transaction revocation. It does not drain detached work, cancel already-invoked I/O or universally guard unrelated generated persistence methods. Operations must be awaited within their owning transaction.
